title: Terminal editors: Vim, Nano and Emacs

videos.script: There is a joke about not being able to leave vim, and this lesson takes it seriously, because the reason it is funny is that it really happens and it happens on a machine somebody is waiting for. {{joke}} You need a terminal editor for a specific reason, and it is not preference. The machine is somewhere else, reached over ssh. There is no graphical anything on it. You are root for ninety seconds to change one line in a configuration file. git just opened something and is waiting for you to write a commit message in it. crontab minus e opened something and will not let you out until you deal with it. In none of those cases do you get to choose. {{why}} So the plan is this. Nano first and completely, because it takes ten minutes and it is enough — the shortcuts are printed at the bottom of the screen and Control X gets you out. Then vim, properly, because it is the one that is on every machine including the broken ones, and because the thing that makes it confusing is one idea rather than a hundred commands. Then emacs, honestly but briefly, because it is genuinely different and you are unlikely to meet it by accident. {{plan}} Every screen in this lesson is a real screen. The editor was started on a real terminal, the keys were really typed, and the screen it drew was captured and then checked against the file on disk, line by line — so a screen that reconstructed wrongly would have been caught rather than published. The swap file warning, the E37 refusal, nano's Save modified buffer prompt: those are what those programs actually printed. {{real}} {{title}}

One edit, start to finish, in vim, on a configuration file — the job you will actually be doing. Change the timeout from thirty to sixty, and get out without breaking anything. {{job}} vim server dot conf. Six lines, and the bottom of the screen says server dot conf, six L, a hundred and one B — six lines, a hundred and one bytes. That bottom line is the only feedback vim gives you and it is worth reading every time. {{open}} Slash timeout, enter. The bottom line now shows the search you typed, and on the right, four comma one: line four, column one. The cursor moved and nothing else happened. {{find}} Now the edit. The cursor is on the t of timeout and the word to change is the one after it, so: w to move onto it, then c w, which is change word, and type sixty, and Escape. The line reads timeout sixty and the position says four comma thirteen. Three keystrokes and a word. Not a selection, not a mouse, not delete-then-retype: an operator and a motion. {{edit}} And here is where people go wrong. Colon w, enter. The bottom line says server dot conf, six L, a hundred and four B, written. Read those numbers. Six lines, same as before — good, nothing was deleted. A hundred and four bytes, three more than a hundred and one, because thirty is two characters and sixty spelled out is five. If you expected to change one word and the line count moved, look at what you actually did before you walk away. {{write}} Then colon q. And if vim refuses — E thirty seven, no write since last change — that is not vim being difficult, it is vim telling you there is work you have not saved. Colon w q does both. Colon q exclamation mark throws the changes away, and you should have a reason before you type it. {{quit}} That is the whole job: open, find, change, write, leave. Four commands and one operator. Everything else in this lesson is a refinement on those five steps. {{whole}}

Three things, and one of them is permission to not learn vim. {{three}} The first is that nano is a legitimate answer. It takes ten minutes, the shortcuts are on the screen, and for the job of changing one line in a configuration file over ssh it does everything you need. Anybody who tells you that is not a real editor is arguing about identity rather than about work. Install it, set EDITOR to it, and move on with your life. {{nano}} The second is that you still have to know four vim commands, because vim is what is there when nano is not — on a rescue image, on a minimal container, on somebody else's machine. Escape gets you to normal mode. Colon q exclamation mark leaves without saving. Colon w q saves and leaves. And u undoes. Four things, and they are the difference between a bad ten minutes and a bad afternoon. {{four}} The third is the idea, if you want the rest of vim: it is a language. An operator and a motion. d is delete and w is a word, so d w deletes a word. c is change, three w is three words, so c three w changes three words. You do not memorise commands, you learn about a dozen operators and a dozen motions and then you can say things neither the manual nor anybody else wrote down. That is the whole of why people who use it will not stop. {{grammar}} And one practical thing that outlives all three. Set EDITOR in your shell profile, deliberately, to whichever of these you chose — because git, crontab minus e, visudo and sudoedit are all going to open something, and the day you find out which one they picked should not be the day you are in a hurry. {{editor}} Lesson thirteen is the last one: cron and systemd timers, and how to make something run at three in the morning without being there. {{next}}
